correctness.rationale: The positive-equilibrium equations are obtained directly from the printed harvested system. For r>m, the predator equilibrium equation defines a unique v=V_q(u), uniformly sends V_q to zero on u in [K/2,K], and gives a sign change of the prey residual between K/2 and K for all sufficiently large q. This proves existence, forces u_q to K, and yields q v_q^(r-m) to e K^p. The exact Jacobian signs then give negative trace and positive determinant for sufficiently large q. For r=m, necessity follows from u<K and sufficiency from a continuous residual sign change. The bundled checker replays the source example but no finite computation is used as proof.

originality.rationale: General predator harvesting, nonlinear harvesting, and local coexistence analysis are prior art and are not claimed as new. The accepted contribution is the source-specific high-harvest theorem: persistence of a stable positive branch with an explicit q-power law when r>m, together with the exact finite coexistence cutoff when r=m. The motivating article gives numerical high-q behavior and leaves a full analysis for future work; targeted source, alias, exponent, and broader-harvesting searches did not locate this dichotomy.
residual_risks: An unindexed note or thesis could contain the same source-specific high-q asymptotic.
The theorem is local at the coexistence branch; it does not eliminate extinction basins or prove global predator persistence.
The source vector field is nonsmooth at population axes for fractional powers, but the accepted Jacobian argument is applied only at strictly positive equilibria.
The r<m regime is not classified.

value.rationale: The motivating article makes harvesting-induced recovery a central conjectural mechanism and explicitly discusses whether predators survive under very high harvesting. The theorem turns that finite-window picture into a structural classification: the sign of r-m decides whether positive coexistence persists to arbitrarily large finite effort or terminates at a finite threshold, and it gives an explicit power law for the residual predator density. This directly informs interpretation of the paper's Example 1 and is more than a routine parameter substitution.
